PAGES 2
=====PAGE 1
AI IN SDLC Assignment 
 
What this assignment is 
You will take one feature from a written specification through to a reviewed pull request on the workshop demo 
repository, using an AI agent to do the work while you hold the checks. The feature itself is small and could be 
hand-written in an afternoon. That is deliberate. What is being asked for is the evidence around it: a context file 
that earns its place, tests that would catch a real mistake, and a judgement call on every review finding. 
Though the assignment is not tied to one vendor. But we suggest going for a free tier of GitHub copilot rather 
than a paid AI tool. Alternatives are welcome as long as it meet's compliance. 
The feature to build 
Add approval limits by role to the invoice approval service in ai-sdlc-demo-app: 
• A Manager may approve invoices up to 50,000. 
• A Director may approve invoices up to 500,000. 
• Anything above 500,000 needs two distinct approvers, and the second approver must be a director. 
• The same user may never count as both approvers on one invoice. 
• A rejected attempt returns a clear reason, and nothing about the invoice changes. 
The last two rules are where an agent is most likely to produce something that looks right and is not. Expect that 
and plan your tests around it. 
 
Note: Use https://github.com/NITIN1670/ai-sdlc-demo-app.git repo for reference.  There is no language 
constraint, so you are free to use any language for this assignment.  
What to do 
1. Set up the context, then show that it matters. Fork the repository and extend AGENTS.md so an agent 
arriving cold knows the approval rules, the layering, the test command and your review expectations. 
2. Use appropriate skills for the agents. 
3. Use appropriate hooks for generating the structured and same format output. 
4. Write the specification with a spec-driven tool. Use Spec Kit, OpenSpec or BMAD, whichever you prefer, 
to produce the specification and task breakdown. Commit the files it generates.  
5. Implement it in at least two steps. Do not ask for the whole feature in a single prompt. Land the single-
approver limits first, with tests, then the two-approver rule. Each step is its own commit, with a message 
that says what changed and why. 
6. Make the tests mean something. 
1. Write the unit tests for the approval rules and review every generated test.  
=====PAGE 2
2. Add one Playwright end-to-end test that covers a rejected over-limit approval through the user 
interface. 
7. Review your own pull request with the agent, then judge the review. Open the pull request, run the 
review prompt from the workshop against the diff, and in the description list every finding with one of 
three verdicts: fixed, dismissed with a reason, or deferred with a reason 
8. Log all AI interactions in a log file - utilizing the capability of skills/hooks. 
9. Create multiple agents and sub-agents for the assignment. 
Install note: mutation testing with Stryker on .NET 8 needs an explicit version. Use dotnet tool install -g 
dotnet-stryker --version 4.13.0. The newest release targets a later runtime and will fail to install. 
The demo video 
Record one demo video of 8 to 10 minutes. Something must run live on screen: a test, the mutation run, the 
end-to-end test. A read-through of files is not a demo. Record with Teams by starting a meeting with only 
yourself and pressing Record, or use any screen recorder that produces an MP4

=================== AGENTS.md
# Project conventions for AI agents

Invoice approval demo app: ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with a small static web UI.

## Layout

- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Domain`: business rules, no web or storage code. `ApprovalService` owns the invoice lifecycle (Draft, PendingApproval, Approved, Rejected).
- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api`: controllers, sign-in (`Auth/`), in-memory repository, and the web UI under `wwwroot/`.
- `backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests`: xUnit tests, one test class per class under test, named `<ClassUnderTest>Tests`.
- `e2e`: Playwright end-to-end tests (`tests/`) and page objects (`pages/`).
- `docs/use-cases`: short briefs for features we may build.

## Conventions

- Controllers live in `Controllers/`, one per resource, route `api/[controller]`. Request bodies are `record` types declared inside the controller.
- Controllers inherit `ApiControllerBase` and use `Handle(...)` so service errors map to 404, 409 and 400.
- Every endpoint is behind sign-in. Restrict actions with `[RequireRole("...")]`: destructive actions are Admin only, approvals are Approver or Admin.
- Business rules go in the Domain project, never in controllers.
- Register services in `Program.cs`. Repositories are interfaces in Domain with an in-memory implementation in Api.
- Every new rule or endpoint needs tests. Use `FakeInvoiceRepository` in tests.
- Use clear names; no one-letter variables or `flag` parameters.
- End-to-end tests use page objects and role-based locators (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`), never CSS or XPath selectors.

## Commands

- Run the app: `dotnet run --project backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api` then open http://localhost:5000
- Run the tests: `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`
- Run end-to-end tests: `cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npm test`

## Demo accounts (not real credentials)

- `demo.approver` / `ChangeMe123!` (role Approver)
- `demo.admin` / `ChangeMe123!` (role Admin)

## Never

- Commit real credentials, tokens or customer data.
- Add business logic to `Program.cs` or controllers.

=================== README.md
# Invoice Approval Demo App

A small invoice approval app used for live AI-in-SDLC demos. It is deliberately simple: a .NET 8 API, a plain web UI, and an in-memory store, so it runs with one command and no database.

## Run it

```
dotnet run --project backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api
```

Open http://localhost:5000 and sign in:

| User | Password | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `demo.approver` | `ChangeMe123!` | Approver |
| `demo.admin` | `ChangeMe123!` | Admin |

These are demo accounts for a local, in-memory app. They are not real credentials.

## What it does

1. Create an invoice (it starts as a draft).
2. Submit it for approval.
3. An approver approves it, or rejects it with a reason.

Invoices move through Draft, Pending Approval, then Approved or Rejected.

## Tests

```
dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln
```

## Project layout

```
backend/
  src/InvoiceApp.Domain   business rules
  src/InvoiceApp.Api      controllers, sign-in, web UI (wwwroot)
  tests/InvoiceApp.Tests  xUnit tests
docs/use-cases            short feature briefs
AGENTS.md                 conventions for AI coding agents
```

## Use cases

- [UC-1 Bulk invoice approval](docs/use-cases/UC-1-bulk-approval.md)
- [UC-2 Partial approval](docs/use-cases/UC-2-partial-approval.md)

# Automate actions with hooks

> Run shell commands automatically when Claude Code edits files, finishes tasks, or needs input. Format code, send notifications, validate commands, and enforce project rules.

Hooks are user-defined shell commands. Claude Code runs them at specific points in its lifecycle, which gives you deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them. Use hooks to enforce project rules, automate repetitive tasks, and integrate Claude Code with your existing tools.

For decisions that require judgment rather than deterministic rules, you can also use [prompt-based hooks](#prompt-based-hooks) or [agent-based hooks](#agent-based-hooks) that use a Claude model to evaluate conditions.

For other ways to extend Claude Code, see [skills](/docs/en/skills) for giving Claude additional instructions and executable commands, [subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents) for running tasks in isolated contexts, and [plugins](/docs/en/plugins/overview) for packaging extensions to share across projects.

<Tip>
  This guide covers common use cases and how to get started. For full event schemas, JSON input/output formats, and advanced features like async hooks and MCP tool hooks, see the [Hooks reference](/docs/en/hooks).
</Tip>

## Set up your first hook

To create a hook, add a `hooks` block to a [settings file](#configure-hook-location). This walkthrough creates a desktop notification hook, so you get alerted whenever Claude is waiting for your input instead of watching the terminal.

## 1. settings.json shape

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "if": "Bash(rm *)",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh",
            "args": []
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Hook handler fields:

| Type | Fields |
| :- | :- |
| All | `type` (required: `"command"`, `"http"`, `"mcp_tool"`, `"prompt"`, `"agent"`), `if`, `timeout`, `statusMessage`, `once` (honored only in skill frontmatter) |
| `command` | `command` (required), `args`, `async`, `asyncRewake`, `shell` (`"bash"` or `"powershell"`), `onFailure` (`"continue"` or `"block"`, v2.1.295+) |
| `http` | `url` (required), `headers`, `allowedEnvVars`, `onFailure` |
| `mcp_tool` | `server`, `tool`, `input` |
| `prompt` / `agent` | `prompt`, `model` |

Timeout defaults are 600s for command, http, and mcp_tool; 30s for prompt; and 60s for agent. The `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool` default drops to 30s on `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreModelSwitch`, and `PostModelSwitch`, and to 10s on `MessageDisplay`.

Matcher rules: `"*"`, `""`, or an omitted matcher matches everything. Values made only of letters, digits, `_`, `-`, spaces, `,`, and `|` are exact matches or lists. Any other character makes the matcher an unanchored JavaScript regex.

## 2. Event names

The page lists 33 events:

- **Per session:** `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `Setup` (`--init-only`, or `--init`/`--maintenance` with `-p`)
- **Per turn:** `UserPromptSubmit`, `UserPromptExpansion`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`
- **Per tool call:** `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PermissionDenied` (auto mode), `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PostToolBatch`
- **Subagents and tasks:** `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle`
- **Other:** `Notification`, `MessageDisplay`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `ConfigChange`, `CwdChanged`, `DirectoryAdded`, `FileChanged`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `PreModelSwitch`, `PostModelSwitch`, `Elicitation`, `ElicitationResult`

## 3. stdin fields

**Common to all events:** `session_id`, `prompt_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `scratchpad_dir`, `permission_mode` (`"default"`, `"plan"`, `"acceptEdits"`, `"auto"`, `"dontAsk"`, `"bypassPermissions"`), `effort` (object with `level`), `hook_event_name`. `agent_id` and `agent_type` appear inside subagents and when using `--agent`.

**Event-specific fields in the excerpt:**

- **PreToolUse:** `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_use_id`
- **SessionStart:** `source` (`"startup"`, `"resume"`, `"clear"`, `"compact"`, `"fork"`), `model` (optional), `agent_type`, `session_title`. On resume or fork with a prior response, also `seconds_since_last_response`, `context_tokens`, `prompt_cache_likely_expired`, `estimated_cache_write_usd`
- **Stop, SubagentStop:** `last_assistant_message` (named in the text, schema not in excerpt)
- **PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch:** `from_model`, `to_model`

**Not in excerpt:** `prompt`, `tool_response`, `stop_hook_active`, `reason`, `trigger`, `custom_instructions`.

This excerpt covers some of the events you asked about, but not all. It doesn't include **SessionEnd**, **PreCompact/PostCompact**, the **hook trust dialog**, or any statement on whether hooks snapshot at session start or reload on change. Those sections are probably elsewhere on the page.

## Stdin fields and examples

### PostToolUse

> `PostToolUse` hooks fire after a tool has already executed successfully. The input includes both `tool_input`, the arguments sent to the tool, and `tool_response`, the result it returned.

Also `duration_ms`: "Optional. Tool execution time in milliseconds. Excludes time spent in permission prompts and PreToolUse hooks."

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "/Users/.../.claude/projects/.../00893aaf-19fa-41d2-8238-13269b9b3ca0.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/Users/...",
  "permission_mode": "default",
  "hook_event_name": "PostToolUse",
  "tool_name": "Write",
  "tool_input": {
    "file_path": "/path/to/file.txt",
    "content": "file content"
  },
  "tool_response": {
    "filePath": "/path/to/file.txt",
    "type": "create"
  },
  "tool_use_id": "toolu_01ABC123...",
  "duration_ms": 12
}
```

### UserPromptSubmit

> UserPromptSubmit hooks receive the `prompt` field containing the submitted text. Pasted content that collapsed to a `[Pasted text #N]` placeholder arrives expanded in place.

They also receive `session_title` when the session has a custom title.

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "/Users/.../.claude/projects/.../00893aaf-19fa-41d2-8238-13269b9b3ca0.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/Users/...",
  "permission_mode": "default",
  "hook_event_name": "UserPromptSubmit",
  "prompt": "Write a function to calculate the factorial of a number"
}
```

### Stop

> Stop hooks receive `stop_hook_active`, `last_assistant_message`, `background_tasks`, and `session_crons`. The `stop_hook_active` field is `true` when Claude Code is already continuing as a result of a stop hook.

> The `last_assistant_message` field contains the text content of Claude's final response, so hooks can access it without parsing the transcript file.

Claude Code also applies "an 8-consecutive-continuation cap" and resets the count when Claude calls a tool. Raise it with `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`.

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "~/.claude/projects/.../00893aaf-19fa-41d2-8238-13269b9b3ca0.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/Users/...",
  "permission_mode": "default",
  "hook_event_name": "Stop",
  "stop_hook_active": true,
  "last_assistant_message": "I've completed the refactoring. Here's a summary...",
  "background_tasks": [
    {
      "id": "task-001",
      "type": "shell",
      "status": "running",
      "description": "tail logs",
      "command": "tail -f /var/log/syslog"
    }
  ],
  "session_crons": [
    {
      "id": "cron-001",
      "schedule": "0 9 * * 1-5",
      "recurring": true,
      "prompt": "check the build"
    }
  ]
}
```

### SubagentStop

> SubagentStop hooks receive `stop_hook_active`, `agent_id`, `agent_type`, `agent_transcript_path`, and `last_assistant_message`. The `agent_type` field is the value used for matcher filtering. The `transcript_path` is the main session's transcript, while `agent_transcript_path` is the subagent's own transcript stored in a nested `subagents/` folder.

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "transcript_path": "~/.claude/projects/.../abc123.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/Users/...",
  "permission_mode": "default",
  "hook_event_name": "SubagentStop",
  "stop_hook_active": false,
  "agent_id": "def456",
  "agent_type": "Explore",
  "agent_transcript_path": "~/.claude/projects/.../abc123/subagents/agent-def456.jsonl",
  "last_assistant_message": "Analysis complete. Found 3 potential issues...",
  "background_tasks": [],
  "session_crons": []
}
```

### SubagentStart

> SubagentStart hooks receive `agent_id` with the unique identifier for the subagent and `agent_type` with the agent name that the matcher filters on.

1338	### Workspace trust
1339	
1340	Claude Code checks workspace trust before it runs any hook from a settings file. What counts as trusted depends on the session type:
1341	
1342	* **Interactive session**: Claude Code holds back hooks from every settings file, including your own `~/.claude/settings.json`, until you accept the [workspace trust dialog](/docs/en/permissions#project-allow-rules-and-workspace-trust) for the folder, or for a parent directory whose trust extends to it
1343	* **`-p` or SDK session**: Claude Code never shows the dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks committed in a repository's `.claude/settings.json` run in a folder you've never trusted
1344	
1345	Before you script `claude -p` over a repository you didn't write, review its `.claude/` settings files, start with [`--bare`](/docs/en/headless#start-faster-with-bare-mode), or [turn hooks off for that run](#disable-or-remove-hooks) with `--settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'`. Frontmatter hooks in a project subagent follow a stricter rule than settings-file hooks. [What runs before you trust a folder](/docs/en/permissions#what-runs-before-you-trust-a-folder) lists each kind of repository content by session type.

1347	### Security best practices
1348	
1349	Keep these practices in mind when writing hooks:
1350	
1351	* **Validate and sanitize inputs**: never trust input data blindly
1352	* **Always quote shell variables**: use `"$VAR"` not `$VAR`
1353	* **Block path traversal**: check for `..` in file paths
1354	* **Use absolute paths**: specify full paths for scripts. In exec form, use `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` and the path needs no quoting. In shell form, wrap it in double quotes
1355	* **Skip sensitive files**: avoid `.env`, `.git/`, keys, etc.

# Run Claude Code programmatically

> Use the Agent SDK to run Claude Code programmatically from the CLI, Python, or TypeScript.

The [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) gives you the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code. It's available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD, or as [Python](/docs/en/agent-sdk/python) and [TypeScript](/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript) packages for full programmatic control.

To run Claude Code in non-interactive mode, pass `-p` with your prompt and the [CLI options](/docs/en/cli-reference) you need:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"
```

This page covers using the Agent SDK via the CLI (`claude -p`). For the Python and TypeScript SDK packages with structured outputs, tool approval callbacks, and native message objects, see the [full Agent SDK documentation](/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview).

## Basic usage

Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag to any `claude` command to run it non-interactively. Not every [CLI option](/docs/en/cli-reference) combines with `-p`. Claude Code rejects `--bg`, and rejects `--cloud` with a task description, with an error naming the conflict; `--cloud` with a session ID and `-p` instead [queues a message into that cloud session](/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web#send-follow-ups-from-the-cli) and exits. Options you'll combine with `-p` often include:

* `--continue` for [continuing conversations](#continue-conversations)
* `--allowedTools` for [auto-approving tools](#auto-approve-tools)
* `--output-format` for [structured output](#get-structured-output)

This example asks Claude a question about your codebase and prints the response:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "What does the auth module do?"
```

Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails, so your scripts can branch on the exit status. If you pass an invalid flag, Claude Code reports the error to stderr before the run starts. When a failure happens inside the run, such as missing authentication, Claude Code prints the failure as the result on stdout.

### Start faster with bare mode

Add `--bare` to reduce startup time by skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, [subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents), installed plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md. Without it, `claude -p` discovers and loads them as an interactive session would, including anything configured in the working directory or `~/.claude`.

Bare mode is useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine. A hook in a teammate's `~/.claude` or an MCP server in the project's `.mcp.json` won't run, because bare mode never reads them. A directory you name with `--add-dir` is a partial exception: bare mode loads skills from its `.claude/skills/` folder, but still skips its `.claude/commands/` and `.claude/agents/` folders. [Skills from additional directories](/docs/en/skills#skills-from-additional-directories) covers what does and doesn't load.

Without `--bare`, a `-p` session runs the hooks in a project's `.claude/settings.json` and connects the servers in its `.mcp.json`, even in a folder you've never trusted. A `-p` session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt. [What runs before you trust a folder](/docs/en/permissions#what-runs-before-you-trust-a-folder) covers each kind of repository content under `-p` and how to keep it out.

This example runs a one-off summarize task in bare mode and pre-approves the Read tool so the call completes without a permission prompt. Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` before running it, because bare mode doesn't use your subscription login:

```bash theme={null}
claude --bare -p "Summarize README.md" --allowedTools "Read"
```

## 1. Where skills live

| Location | Path | Scope |
| :- | :- | :- |
| Enterprise | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in the managed settings directory | All users where your organization deploys it |
| Personal | `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | All your projects on this machine |
| Project | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | This repository; commit it to share |
| Nested | `<subdir>/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | Sessions in or below `<subdir>` |
| Additional directory | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in a directory passed with `--add-dir` | That session |
| Plugin | `<plugin>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | Where the plugin is enabled, as `/plugin-name:skill-name` |

On name collisions, enterprise beats personal, and personal beats project. A skill also beats a same-named file in `.claude/commands/`. Plugin skills are namespaced, so they don't collide.

## 2. Frontmatter fields

Every field is optional, and `description` is the only one recommended. Field names must match exactly, and unrecognized fields are ignored without an error. Frontmatter is read only if the opening `---` is the file's first line. Booleans accept `true`/`false`, and also `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off`/`1`/`0` in v2.1.218 or later.

| Field | Description |
| :- | :- |
| `name` | Command name in the `/` menu. Defaults to the directory name. |
| `description` | What the skill does and when to use it. Claude uses it to decide when to load the skill. |
| `when_to_use` | Extra trigger context. Appended to `description` and counts toward the same cap. |
| `argument-hint` | Autocomplete hint, such as `[issue-number]`. |
| `arguments` | Named positional arguments for `$name` substitution. |
| `disable-model-invocation` | `true` stops Claude from loading the skill automatically. Default `false`. |
| `user-invocable` | `false` hides the skill from the `/` menu so only Claude invokes it. Default `true`. |
| `allowed-tools` | Tools usable without a permission prompt during the invoking turn. |
| `disallowed-tools` | Tools removed from the available pool while the skill is active. |
| `model` | Model override for the current turn. |
| `effort` | Effort level: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. |
| `context` | `fork` runs the skill in a forked subagent. |
| `agent` | Subagent type used when `context: fork` is set. |
| `background` | With `context: fork`, `false` waits for the result. Default `true`. |
| `hooks` | Hooks registered when the skill is invoked. |
| `paths` | Glob patterns limiting automatic activation. |
| `shell` | `bash` (default) or `powershell` for `` !`command` `` injection. |
| `metadata`, `license`, `compatibility` | Informational fields that Claude Code accepts but doesn't act on. |

Outside Claude Code (claude.ai uploads, the Skills API), only `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, and `allowed-tools` are accepted. Other keys cause a hard error.

Example from the page:

```yaml
---
name: my-skill
description: What this skill does
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Read Grep
---
```

## 3. Invocation control

| Frontmatter | You can invoke | Claude can invoke | Description in context |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| (default) | Yes | Yes | Always |
| `disable-model-invocation: true` | Yes | Not on its own | No |
| `user-invocable: false` | No | Yes | Always |

Claude can invoke a skill that has `disable-model-invocation: true` only if you invoke it first.

## 4. Supporting files

Yes, skills can include other files. `SKILL.md` should reference them so Claude knows when to load them:

detail:
## 1. Locations and precedence

| Priority | Location | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (highest) | Managed settings | Organization-wide |
| 2 | `--agents` CLI flag | Current session |
| 3 | `.claude/agents/` | Current project |
| 4 | `~/.claude/agents/` | All your projects |
| 5 (lowest) | Plugin's `agents/` directory | Where the plugin is enabled |

"When multiple subagents share the same name, Claude Code uses the one from the higher-priority location."

- Project subagents are found by walking up from the current working directory, so every `.claude/agents/` between there and the repository root is scanned. If nested directories define the same `name`, the one closest to the working directory wins.
- `.claude/agents/` and `~/.claude/agents/` are scanned recursively. Identity comes only from the `name` field, not the path.
- Within one directory tree, duplicate names are not resolved by precedence: Claude Code loads only one, "chosen by filesystem read order." `/doctor` reports these.
- Plugin subfolders become part of the identifier. `agents/review/security.md` in plugin `my-plugin` registers as `my-plugin:review:security`.
- Directories added with `--add-dir` also contribute their `.claude/agents/`.

## 2. Frontmatter fields

Only `name` and `description` are required. Field names are camelCase and must match exactly. Unrecognized fields are ignored without an error.

| Field | Required | Type / values | Description (quoted where the page gives it) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | Yes | string, max 256 chars | Unique identifier. Can't contain `:`, which is reserved for plugin-scoped names. |
| `description` | Yes | string | "When Claude should delegate to this subagent" |
| `tools` | No | comma-separated string or YAML list | Allowlist. "Inherits every tool available to subagents if omitted." |
| `disallowedTools` | No | same format as `tools` | Denylist, applied to the inherited or specified list. |
| `model` | No | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full model ID, or `inherit` | Omitted means the model order in section 4 applies. |
| `permissionMode` | No | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, `plan` (`manual` = `default`) | Ignored for plugin subagents. If the main conversation is in `bypassPermissions`, `acceptEdits`, or auto mode, that mode applies instead. |
| `maxTurns` | No | number | "Maximum number of agentic turns before the subagent stops." |
| `skills` | No | list | Skills whose "full content is injected" at startup, up to 32 distinct names. |
| `mcpServers` | No | list of server-name strings or inline definitions | "MCP servers available to this subagent." Ignored for plugin subagents. |
| `hooks` | No | object | "Lifecycle hooks scoped to this subagent." Ignored for plugin subagents. |
| `memory` | No | `user`, `project`, `local` | "Persistent memory scope... Enables cross-session learning." |
| `background` | No | boolean | "Set to `true` to keep this subagent in the background even when Claude asks to wait for it." |
| `effort` | No | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` | Overrides the session effort level, but not the `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` variable. |
| `isolation` | No | `worktree` | Runs the subagent in a temporary git worktree, branched by default from your default branch. Cleaned up automatically if no changes are made. |
| `color` | No | `red`, `blue`, `green`, `yellow`, `purple`, `orange`, `pink`, `cyan` | Display color in the task list and transcript. |
| `initialPrompt` | No | string | Auto-submitted first turn when the agent runs as the main session agent (`--agent` or `agent` setting). Ignored for plugin subagents. |
| `omitClaudeMd` | No | boolean | Starts without user, project, and local CLAUDE.md files. Requires v2.1.271+. |
| `autoCompactWindow` | No | integer, 100000–1000000 | Lowers this subagent's auto-compact window. Requires v2.1.296+. |

# CLI reference

> Complete reference for Claude Code command-line interface, including commands and flags.

## CLI commands

You can start sessions, pipe content, resume conversations, and manage updates with these commands:

| Command | Description | Example |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `claude` | Start interactive session | `claude` |
| `claude "query"` | Start interactive session with initial prompt | `claude "explain this project"` |
| `claude -p "query"` | Query via SDK, then exit | `claude -p "explain this function"` |
| `cat file \| claude -p "query"` | Process piped content | `cat logs.txt \| claude -p "explain"` |
| `claude -c` | Continue most recent conversation in current directory | `claude -c` |
| `claude -c -p "query"` | Continue via SDK | `claude -c -p "Check for type errors"` |
| `claude -r "<session>" "query"` | Resume session by ID or name | `claude -r "auth-refactor" "Finish this PR"` |
| `claude update` | Update to latest version | `claude update` |
| `claude gateway` | Start the self-hosted [Claude apps gateway](/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway) server, for administrators deploying SSO and policy in front of Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. Requires `--config` pointing at a [`gateway.yaml`](/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway-config). | `claude gateway --config gateway.yaml` |
| `claude install [version]` | Install or reinstall the native binary. Accepts a version like `2.1.118`, or `stable` or `latest`. See [Install a specific version](/docs/en/setup#install-a-specific-version) | `claude install stable` |

| `claude auth logout` | Log out from your Anthropic account | `claude auth logout` |
| `claude auth status` | Show authentication status as JSON. Use `--text` for human-readable output. Exits with code 0 if logged in, 1 if not. The JSON includes a `configDirectory` field naming the [configuration directory](/docs/en/claude-directory) the CLI uses. The field requires Claude Code v2.1.268 or later. The JSON's `authMethod` field is one of `none`, `claude.ai`, `oauth_token`, `api_key`, `api_key_helper`, or `third_party` | `claude auth status` |
| `claude agents` | Open [agent view](/docs/en/agent-view) to monitor and dispatch parallel background sessions. The official GitHub docs confirm that Copilot supports `preToolUse` hooks, but they don't specify a single `hooks.json` filename or exit-code behavior.

- **Scope and location:** Hooks enable you to execute custom shell commands at strategic points in an agent's workflow. They work with the cloud agent and the Copilot CLI. Repository hooks go in JSON files, stored in your repository at .github/hooks/*.json, so the docs use a glob rather than one fixed `hooks.json`. The CLI also reads personal hooks from your home directory at ~/.copilot/hooks/*.json.
- **preToolUse:** Official docs say hooks can programmatically approve or deny tool executions.
- **Exit codes (community source, not official):** A community mirror of GitHub's awesome-copilot Learning Hub says exit code 0 approves, exit code 2 explicitly denies (v1.0.70+), and other non-zero codes signal a script error. Exit code 2 is recommended for deliberate policy blocks, while exit code 1 signals an unexpected script error. Older revisions of the same mirror describe any non-zero exit as a denial, so verify this against the official docs.
- **Other capabilities:** The same mirror says preToolUse hooks can also modify tool arguments before they are passed to the tool, and can inject extra context into the agent's reasoning.
- **Events:** The mirror lists events including preToolUse, postToolUse, agentStop, subagentStop, errorOccurred, plus sessionStart from the official docs.
- **Limits:** A third-party Enkrypt doc says hooks work with Copilot Coding Agent and Copilot CLI, but NOT with VS Code Copilot Chat or inline suggestions.

I didn't find an official 2026 schema for the hook config file itself, so check docs.github.com before relying on field names or exit-code behavior.

I ran one search. It didn't return the official GitHub docs page, so these details come from third-party pages and a GitHub blog post. Check them against the docs before relying on them.

- **Format:** Custom agents are Markdown files (*.agent.md) that configure GitHub Copilot with a persona, tool access, guardrails, and an optional model preference.
- **Naming conflict:** The GitHub blog describes custom agents defined in agents.md files, and each agents.md file acts as an agent persona, which you define with frontmatter and custom instructions. - **Location:** One community guideline says the .github/agents/ directory (repository-level) or agents/ directory (organization/enterprise-level).

- **Official docs URL:** Third-party files cite https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/create-custom-agents. I did not open this page, so it is unverified.
- **Usage:** In VS Code, open Copilot Chat and use the agent picker dropdown at the top of the chat panel. In Copilot CLI, custom agents are discoverable via the agent picker inside a session.
- **Staleness warning:** One guide says the CLI went GA in February 2026 and ships updates constantly, so commands, flags, file locations, and customization behavior change often.

The main open question is whether the official frontmatter schema matches the field list above, and whether the file pattern is *.agent.md or agents.md. The official docs page should settle both.

## 1. "Failed hooks on Windows without Git Bash" (verbatim)

> If the error for a blocked tool call includes this text, a `PreToolUse` or `PermissionRequest` command hook failed or timed out and blocked the call:
>
> ```text
> blocking because Git Bash wasn't found and this hook doesn't set "shell" to "powershell", so only exit code 0 or 2 counts as its verdict.
> ```
>
> A shell-form hook with no `shell` set runs in PowerShell when Git Bash isn't installed, and a script written for Bash may not run as written there. Pick the fix that matches your hook:
>
> * **The hook is written for Bash**: install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win), or set [`CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH`](/docs/en/env-vars) if Git Bash is installed where Claude Code doesn't find it, then start a new session
> * **The hook runs one `.exe`, not a `.cmd` or `.bat` file**: put the program in `command` and its arguments in `args` to use [exec form](#exec-form-and-shell-form), and add [`"onFailure": "block"`](#block-the-action-when-a-hook-fails). Claude Code then starts the program with no shell. Without `"onFailure": "block"`, the call can go ahead when the program fails, is missing, or times out
> * **The hook is written for PowerShell**: add `"shell": "powershell"` and [`"onFailure": "block"`](#block-the-action-when-a-hook-fails) to the hook. Without `"onFailure": "block"`, the call can go ahead when the hook still fails or times out. To find out why the hook failed, check the [debug log](#debug-hooks)
> * **The action should go ahead when the hook fails**: add `"onFailure": "continue"` to the hook
>
> For a hook that shows this error, any exit code other than 0 or 2 counts as a [failure](#block-the-action-when-a-hook-fails), even when the hook prints JSON that doesn't deny the call.

The excerpt has `decision control` subsections for PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop. SubagentStop has no subsection of its own, so its text is quoted from its section.

#### PostToolUse decision control

`PostToolUse` hooks can provide feedback to Claude after tool execution. In addition to the [JSON output fields](#json-output) available to all hooks, your hook script can return these event-specific fields:

| Field | Description |
| :- | :- |
| `decision` | `"block"` adds the `reason` next to the tool result. Claude still sees the original output; to replace it, use `updatedToolOutput` |
| `reason` | Explanation shown to Claude when `decision` is `"block"` |
| `additionalContext` | String added to Claude's context alongside the tool result. See [Add context for Claude](#add-context-for-claude) |
| `classifierContext` | Short note about this call's result for the [auto mode](/docs/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) classifier rather than for Claude. See [Annotate a result for the auto mode classifier](#annotate-a-result-for-the-auto-mode-classifier). Requires Claude Code v2.1.236 or later |
| `updatedToolOutput` | Replaces the tool's output with the provided value before it is sent to Claude. The value must match the tool's output shape |
| `updatedMCPToolOutput` | Replaces the output for [MCP tools](#match-mcp-tools) only. Prefer `updatedToolOutput`, which works for all tools |

The example below replaces the output of a `Bash` call. The replacement value matches the `Bash` tool's output shape:

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
    "additionalContext": "Additional information for Claude",
    "updatedToolOutput": {
      "stdout": "[redacted]",
      "stderr": "",
      "interrupted": false,
      "isImage": false
    }
  }
}
```

The warning that follows the example:

> `updatedToolOutput` only changes what Claude sees. The tool has already run by the time the hook fires, so any files written, commands executed, or network requests sent have already taken effect. Telemetry such as OpenTelemetry tool spans and analytics events also captures the original output before the hook runs. To prevent or modify a tool call before it runs, use a [PreToolUse](#pretooluse) hook instead.
>
> The replacement value must match the tool's output shape. Built-in tools return structured objects rather than plain strings. For example, `Bash` returns an object with `stdout`, `stderr`, `interrupted`, and `isImage` fields. For built-in tools, a value that doesn't match the tool's output schema is ignored and the original output is used. MCP tool output is passed through without schema validation. Stripping error details that Claude needs can cause it to proceed on a false assumption.

#### UserPromptSubmit decision control

`UserPromptSubmit` hooks can control whether a submitted prompt is processed and add context. All [JSON output fields](#json-output) are available.

There are two ways to add context to the conversation on exit code 0:

* **Plain text stdout**: Claude Code adds stdout it [treats as plain text](#exit-code-0) to Claude's context
* **JSON with `additionalContext`**: use the JSON format below for more control. The `additionalContext` field is added as context

Neither channel produces a visible transcript entry. Plain stdout and the `additionalContext` value are each injected as a system reminder that starts with the hook's name; Claude reads both. To confirm delivery, check the [debug log](#debug-hooks).

To block a prompt, return a JSON object with `decision` set to `"block"`:

| Field | Description |
| :- | :- |
| `decision` | `"block"` stops the prompt before it reaches Claude. Omit to allow the prompt to proceed |
| `reason` | Shown to the user when `decision` is `"block"`. Not added to context |
| `additionalContext` | String added to Claude's context alongside the submitted prompt. See [Add context for Claude](#add-context-for-claude) |

## Custom agent profiles: key details

**File location and naming**
- The agents tab creates a template at `.github/agents/my-agent.agent.md` in the target repository, which implies the `<name>.agent.md` pattern. The page doesn't state the pattern as a general rule.
- Filenames may use only letters, digits, dots, hyphens, and underscores. "the filename may only contain the following characters" (quoted from the page).
- Organization-level profiles go in the organization's `.github` or `.github-private` repository, and enterprise-level profiles go in the `.github-private` repository of an organization designated in enterprise settings. For either level, remove the `.github/` portion so the file sits in a root `agents` directory.
- The profile must be committed and merged into the default branch before it appears in the dropdown.

**YAML frontmatter fields**

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | No | Defaults to the filename without the `.md` or `.agent.md` suffix. |
| `description` | Yes | Explains what the agent does and its domain expertise. |
| `tools` | No | List of tool names or aliases, including MCP tools (e.g., `server/tool`). If omitted, all available tools are enabled. |
| `mcp-servers` | No | MCP servers available only to this agent. |
| `model` | No | Selects the AI model. The page limits this to VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, and Xcode. |
| `target` | No | `vscode` or `github-copilot`. If omitted, the agent is available in both. |
| `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `infer` | Not covered | These fields don't appear on this page. See the Custom agents configuration reference. |

The Markdown body below the frontmatter contains the prompt, up to 30,000 characters.

**Invocation by other agents or subagent delegation:** This page doesn't address it.

**Supported surfaces**
- **GitHub.com / cloud agent:** Select the agent from the agents tab or panel dropdown, or choose it when assigning an issue. Pull requests note which custom agent did the work. The page says agents work "wherever Copilot cloud agent is available."
- **GitHub Copilot CLI:** Use the `/agent` slash command, reference the agent in a prompt, or pass it as a command-line argument.
- **VS Code:** The page references the `model` field and the `vscode` target value but gives no separate setup steps.
- **JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, and Xcode:** Custom agents are in public preview and subject to change.

**Verbatim example (testing specialist, frontmatter only)**

The full example body exceeds the 125-character quote limit, so I've included only the frontmatter. The body defines a testing-focused role that analyzes coverage gaps, writes and reviews tests, and avoids changing production code unless asked. The example omits `tools`, so it has access to all tools.

```
---
name: test-specialist
description: Focuses on test coverage, quality, and testing best practices without modifying production code
---
```

**Page date:** Not shown on the page.

## Custom Agent Location and Format

- **Workspace (Copilot):** `.github/agents`, with `.agent.md` or `.md` files.
- **Workspace (Claude format):** `.claude/agents`, with `.md` files in the Claude agent format.
- **User (Copilot):** `~/.copilot/agents`, with `.agent.md` or `.md` files.
- **User (Anthropic Claude):** `~/.claude/agents`, with `.md` files in the Claude format.
- **Local harness:** User-level agents are stored in VS Code profile storage, not in the harness folders.
- **Legacy files:** Older `.chatmode.md` files should be renamed to `.agent.md`.

## Frontmatter Attributes Named on the Page

- **`name`**: Sets the display name, such as `name: Planner`.
- **`description`**: Summarizes the agent's purpose.
- **`tools`**: Restricts available tools. If set, only the listed tools are available.
- **`user-invocable`**: Set to `false` to hide the agent from the agents dropdown while keeping it available as a subagent. This applies to both Local and Copilot harnesses.
- **`disable-model-invocation`**: Controls subagent invocation. The page gives no further detail.
- **`handoffs`**: A list of entries with `label`, `agent`, `prompt`, and `send`. Handoffs are described for the Local harness. The page says `send: true` submits the prompt automatically.

The page doesn't cover `argument-hint`, `agents`, `model` (as a key), `target`, or `mcp-servers`. It defers to the Custom Agent File Reference for the full field list.

## Subagents

The page says another agent can run a custom agent as a subagent. It doesn't name an `agents` attribute or a `runSubagent`/`agent` tool. Handoffs switch the active agent, while subagents delegate work without switching.

## Agent Skills

The page doesn't mention a `.github/skills/` path. It lists Agent Skills as one customization option alongside prompt files and custom agents. It also says the diagnostics view shows loaded skills and links to a separate Agent Skills article.

## AGENTS.md

The page doesn't mention `AGENTS.md`.

## Example (Planner Agent)

The example is saved as `.github/agents/planner.agent.md`. Its frontmatter lines are:

- "name: Planner"
- "description: Generate an implementation plan without changing code"
- "tools: ['read', 'search']"

The body includes: "Do not edit files. Return a Markdown plan with these sections:"

A handoff example adds `label`, `agent`, `prompt`, and `send` entries, with `send: false` by default.

## Date and Preview Notes

- The Agent Customizations editor is labeled **(Preview)**.
- The page footer shows **10/14/2026**.
- Custom agents were previously called custom chat modes, and the functionality is unchanged.
- The `chat.agentFilesLocations` and `chat.modeFilesLocations` settings are deprecated and apply only to the Local harness.
- Organization-level custom agent discovery is enabled by default. It can be disabled with `github.copilot.chat.organizationCustomAgents.enabled`.

**Location**
- **Workspace:** the `.github/prompts` folder. The page calls this the "`.github/prompts` folder."
- **User level:** your VS Code profile's user data. The page gives no fixed path.
- The Local harness uses these locations.

**File format**
- Extension: "Prompt files are Markdown files with the `.prompt.md` extension."
- An optional YAML frontmatter header configures the prompt. The Markdown body holds the prompt text.

**Frontmatter fields (all optional)**
- `description`: a short description of the prompt.
- `name`: the name you type after `/` in chat. Defaults to the file name.
- `argument-hint`: hint text shown in the chat input to tell users what to enter.
- `agent`: `ask`, `agent`, `plan`, or a custom agent name. Defaults to the current agent, but becomes `agent` if `tools` is set.
- `model`: the language model to use. Defaults to the model selected in the model picker.
- `tools`: tools, tool sets, MCP tools, or extension tools. `<server name>/*` includes all tools from one MCP server. Unavailable tools are ignored.

**Invocation**
- In the Chat view with **Local** selected, type `/` and the prompt name. You can add input after the name.
- Alternatives: the **Chat: Run Prompt** command, or the play button in the editor title for an open prompt file.
- Agent skills also appear as slash commands.

**Copilot CLI and cloud agent**
- The page doesn't mention Copilot CLI or cloud agent by name.
- It says prompt files "run only in **Local** harness sessions in the Chat view." For other harnesses, it recommends creating an agent skill instead.

**Example (excerpts from the React form example)**

detail:
**Source:** "About hooks for GitHub Copilot." The page shows no date or version.

**1. File locations**
- **Repository:** `.github/hooks/*.json`. The page says these apply to Copilot agents used in that repository.
- **Personal (Copilot CLI only):** `~/.copilot/hooks/*.json`, which applies whenever you use Copilot CLI.
- **Inconsistency:** The example is described as living in "`~/.github/hooks/project-hooks.json` within a repository," which doesn't match the repository path above.

**2. Config schema**
- **Top level:** `version` (must be `1`) and `hooks` (an object whose keys are event names and whose values are arrays of hook objects).
- **Event names (exact casing):** `sessionStart`, `sessionEnd`, `userPromptSubmitted`, `preToolUse`, `postToolUse`, `agentStop`, `subagentStop`, `errorOccurred`

**Per-hook fields:**

| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | Yes | Must be `"command"` |
| `bash` | Yes on Unix | "Path to the bash script to execute" |
| `powershell` | Yes on Windows | "Path to the PowerShell script to execute" |
| `cwd` | No | Relative to repository root |
| `env` | No | Merged with the existing environment |
| `timeoutSec` | No | "Maximum execution time in seconds (default: 30)" |

The page does not define `command` or `timeout` keys. The command is set through `bash` and `powershell`, and the timeout key is `timeoutSec`. The field descriptions say "path," but the example uses inline commands (for instance, an `echo` redirected to a log file), so the values may be command strings.

**3. Stdin input fields per event:** Not specified. The page says hooks receive "detailed information about agent actions via JSON input," but it lists no fields for any event. It points to a separate hooks reference that isn't included.

**4. Exit codes and output semantics:** Not specified. The page says `preToolUse` "can approve or deny tool executions," but it doesn't explain how a hook signals approval or denial (exit codes or JSON output). It also doesn't mention `modifiedArgs` or `additionalContext`.

**5. Shell and platform options:** The only platform-specific keys are `bash` (Unix) and `powershell` (Windows). The page describes no other shell option. Each key is required on its platform, so a config that runs on both needs both.

**6. Supported surfaces:** Copilot cloud agent on GitHub and GitHub Copilot CLI in the terminal. The page doesn't mention VS Code.

**7. Example config:** The full example is longer than the 125-character quote limit, so I can't quote it verbatim. In summary, it defines:
- `sessionStart`: appends a timestamped message to a log file.
- `userPromptSubmitted`: runs a logging script with an environment variable set.
- `preToolUse`: runs a security check and a logging script. The security check has a short excerpt, `"timeoutSec": 15`.
- `postToolUse`: appends results to a JSONL file.
- `sessionEnd`: runs a cleanup script with a longer timeout.

detail:
The page has no file-by-surface matrix, no CLI or VS Code details, and no product size limits. The summary below comes from what the page does say. Quoting the full lists would exceed the 125-character limit, so I've used short excerpts and paraphrased the rest.

**Supported files**

| File | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | Repository `.github` directory | Repository-wide guidance for requests in the repo |
| `.github/instructions/NAME.instructions.md` | `.github/instructions`, including subdirectories | Path-specific; requires `applyTo` frontmatter |
| `AGENTS.md` | Anywhere in the repo | Agent instructions; the nearest file in the directory tree wins |
| `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md` | Repository root only | Single-file alternative for agent instructions |

**Frontmatter**

- `applyTo` takes comma-separated glob patterns, such as `"**/*.ts,**/*.tsx"`. It uses "glob syntax to specify what files or directories the instructions apply to."
- `excludeAgent` accepts `"code-review"` or `"cloud-agent"` to stop that surface from reading the file. If it's omitted, "both Copilot code review and Copilot cloud agent will use your instructions."
- The page says path-specific instructions are "only supported for Copilot cloud agent and Copilot code review" on GitHub.com.

**Which surfaces read them**

- **Copilot code review:** Reads repository-wide and path-specific instructions, plus agent instructions and skills. It reads them from the head branch, "not the base branch." Custom instructions are on by default and can be toggled under "Use custom instructions when reviewing pull requests."
- **Copilot cloud agent:** Reads repository-wide, path-specific, and agent instructions. The page says agent instructions "are used by AI agents."
- **Copilot Chat on github.com:** The page names only `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. It appears in the References list when used.
- **Copilot CLI and VS Code Chat:** Not covered. The page only links to a separate IDE article.

**Precedence**

- Repository-wide and matching path-specific files both apply: "the instructions from both files are used."
- For agent instructions, "the nearest AGENTS.md file in the directory tree will take precedence."
- Across instruction types, personal instructions rank first, then repository, then organization. "all sets of relevant instructions are provided to Copilot."
- The page advises avoiding conflicting instructions.

**Size limits**

The page sets no product size limit. The only length cap, "Instructions must be no longer than 2 pages," appears in the onboarding prompt for generating `copilot-instructions.md` with cloud agent. It is a guideline for that task, not a platform limit.

# How Claude remembers your project

> Give Claude persistent instructions with CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files, and let Claude accumulate learnings automatically with auto memory.

Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window. Two mechanisms carry knowledge across sessions:

* **CLAUDE.md files**: instructions you write to give Claude persistent context. Claude can also read a repository's [`AGENTS.md` files](#agents-md) in place of CLAUDE.md
* **Auto memory**: notes Claude writes itself based on your corrections and preferences

This page covers how to:

* [Write and organize CLAUDE.md files](#claude-md-files)
* [Use an existing AGENTS.md](#agents-md) as your project instructions
* [Scope rules to specific file types](#organize-rules-with-claude/rules/) with `.claude/rules/`
* [Configure auto memory](#auto-memory) so Claude takes notes automatically
* [Troubleshoot](#troubleshoot-memory-issues) when instructions aren't being followed

## CLAUDE.md vs auto memory

Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation. Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a [PreToolUse hook](/docs/en/hooks-guide) instead. The more specific and concise your instructions, the more consistently Claude follows them.

| | CLAUDE.md files | Auto memory |
| :- | :- | :- |
| **Who writes it** | You | Claude |
| **What it contains** | Instructions and rules | Learnings and patterns |
| **Scope** | Project, user, or org | Per repository, shared across worktrees |
| **Loaded into** | Every session | Every session (first 200 lines or 25KB) |

The official GitHub docs cover this topic, along with Microsoft's Visual Studio docs and some community guides.

- **What skills are:** GitHub's docs describe skills as bundles of instructions, scripts, and assets that Copilot pulls in on demand for specialized work. Agent skills work with Copilot cloud agent, the GitHub Copilot CLI, and agent mode in Visual Studio Code.
- **Where they live:** For repository-specific skills, the docs point to .github/skills/, .claude/skills/, .agents/skills/. Personal skills go under ~/.copilot/skills/, ~/.claude/skills/, ~/.agents/skills/. Repository skills are shared with a team through source control, while personal skills stay out of any repo.
- **SKILL.md format:** Each skill gets its own subdirectory with a SKILL.md file. The file uses Markdown with YAML frontmatter. The name and description fields are the required frontmatter entries. The name should be lowercase and hyphenated, and typically matches the directory name.
- **Activation:** When you use agent mode, Copilot automatically discovers skills from your repository and user profile. The agent decides when a skill is relevant to your request and activates it.
- **Optional resources:** Community guidance suggests optional subfolders such as scripts/, references/, assets/, and templates/. Reference docs in references/ are read into context when the skill points to them, while assets/ files are used as-is in output (Example Files).

Caveat: the top result is an internal Forge project page (docs.platformdev.saif.com), not GitHub's documentation, so its specifics apply only to that repo. The community awesome-copilot guide is also not official. For authoritative details, use docs.github.com's "create skills" page.

The official GitHub docs cover CLI instructions well. The results did not include official pages for CLI custom agents or CLI hooks, so those points are less certain.

**Instruction files (official docs)**
- The CLI auto-loads AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md from the repository, or $HOME/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md from your home directory.
- Setting the COPILOT_CUSTOM_INSTRUCTIONS_DIRS variable to a list of folders makes the CLI also check those folders for AGENTS.md and any .github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md files.
- Path-specific instructions only apply when their applyTo pattern matches files the CLI is working on, and an instruction file that you disable using /instructions is not included.
- Files can pull in others with @ references. The CLI reads the referenced file immediately and supports references within referenced files.
- The --no-custom-instructions flag skips loading these files (avoid loading these instructions).

**Custom agents and hooks (less verified)**
- The main agent can hand work to a subagent that uses a custom agent profile. Examples include a reviewer, docs writer, or security auditor ().
- Plugins can bundle skills, hooks, custom agents, and MCP servers ().
- A third-party awesome-copilot mirror describes hooks in .github/hooks/ with a hooks.json file and events such as preToolUse and postToolUse. It links to the coding agent hooks spec, so it may describe the cloud coding agent rather than the CLI ().

**Caveats**
- A personal blog (srisatyalokesh.is-a.dev) shows .github/agents and gh copilot agent/skill register commands. These don't appear in the official snippets, and the npm package it names looks outdated. I'd treat that post as unreliable.
- One blog notes that the CLI reached GA in February 2026 and changes often, and that its July 2026 checks should be re-verified against the official docs ().

**Instruction files**

- **`.github/copilot-instructions.md`**: "For Copilot sessions, use `.github/copilot-instructions.md` for project-wide guidance." Personal Copilot instructions go in `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md`.
- **`.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`**: Targeted files, searched recursively. Frontmatter fields are `name`, `description`, and `applyTo`. Activation can be by file pattern, task relevance, or manual attachment.
- **`AGENTS.md`**: "`AGENTS.md` is a cross-agent format for project guidance." "Multiple harnesses, including Copilot and OpenAI Codex, support it." The Local harness also supports it. Place the primary file at the repository root.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**: "For Anthropic Claude sessions, use `CLAUDE.md` at the repository root for project-wide guidance." For the Local harness, it also checks `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and `CLAUDE.local.md`.
- **`.claude/rules`**: For Claude rules files, "use a `paths` property instead of `applyTo` for glob patterns."

**Nested AGENTS.md**

Nested files are used for folder-specific guidance. Discovery and activation follow the selected harness's rules. For the Local harness, when `chat.useNestedAgentsMdFiles` is enabled, "VS Code lists these files with their folder locations." The page also notes that multiple `.instructions.md` files with different `applyTo` patterns can serve as an alternative.

**Settings (Local harness)**

- `chat.useAgentsMdFile`: "to enable or disable support for `AGENTS.md` files."
- `chat.useNestedAgentsMdFiles`: "controls support for nested `AGENTS.md` files and is disabled by default."
- `chat.useClaudeMdFile`: "To enable or disable support for `CLAUDE.md` files."
- `github.copilot.chat.codeGeneration.useInstructionFiles`: "The Local harness also discovers this workspace file when" this setting is enabled.
- Also referenced: `chat.includeApplyingInstructions`, `chat.includeReferencedInstructions`, `chat.useCustomizationsInParentRepositories`, `github.copilot.chat.organizationInstructions.enabled`.

**Preview and status labels**

- **Experimental**: Nested AGENTS.md files. "is experimental and might change or be removed."
- **Deprecated**: `chat.instructionsFilesLocations` "adds other locations for the Local harness only." Settings-based code and test generation instructions "are deprecated as of VS Code 1.102."
- No "Preview" label appears on the page.

The page does not state default values for `chat.useAgentsMdFile` or `chat.useClaudeMdFile`.

summary: WebFetch: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/create-custom-agents-for-cli
detail:
**Source:** The page is available and is a GitHub Docs article on creating and using custom agents in Copilot CLI.

**Where profiles are loaded from**
- **Project:** `.github/agents/`
- **User:** `~/.copilot/agents/`
- If a personal and a repository agent share the same ID, the personal agent is used.
- The ID is the file name without `.agent.md` or `.md`. Files in subdirectories of `agents` include the subdirectory in the ID, joined with `--`. For example, `agents/security/security-auditor.agent.md` becomes `security--security-auditor`.
- `.claude/agents` is not mentioned. The page does reference `CLAUDE.md`, but only as a repository instruction file.

**Frontmatter fields**
The page's examples show four fields. It doesn't list the full schema and refers to the Custom agents configuration reference for that.
- `name`: optional. Its value can be used with `--agent` in place of the ID. It doesn't affect duplicate resolution.
- `description`: explains the agent's expertise and when to use it. Copilot uses this for inference.
- `tools`: restricts tool access. Agents have access to all tools by default. The example uses `tools: ["*"]`.
- `include-custom-instructions`: when set to `true`, a subagent follows the repository's custom instructions. This setting has no effect when you select the agent yourself.

**Delegation to other agents**
The page doesn't say whether a custom agent can delegate to other agents. It does say that custom agent work runs in a temporary subagent with its own context window, while the main agent handles planning and coordination.

**Selecting an agent**
- **Slash command:** Enter `/agent` in interactive mode, choose an agent from the list, then enter your prompt.
- **Explicit instruction:** Name the agent in your prompt.
- **By inference:** Copilot selects an agent based on its description. A profile can also define a trigger word.
- **Command line:** Use `--agent`. The page gives this verbatim example:

```shell
copilot --agent security-auditor --prompt "Check /src/app/validator.go"
```

The `--agent` value can also be a quoted `name` value, such as a name containing spaces.

**Per-agent hooks**
The page doesn't mention hooks.

summary: WebFetch: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/create-skills
detail:
## Skill locations

- **Project skills** (one repository): `.github/skills`, `.claude/skills`, or `.agents/skills` in the repo.
- **Personal skills** (all projects): `~/.copilot/skills` or `~/.agents/skills` in your home directory.

Each skill needs its own subdirectory, named in lowercase with hyphens. The instruction file must be named exactly `SKILL.md`.

## SKILL.md frontmatter

- **`name`** (required): A unique, lowercase, hyphenated identifier. It usually matches the directory name.
- **`description`** (required): Explains what the skill does and when Copilot should use it.
- **`license`** (optional): Describes the license that applies to the skill.
- **`allowed-tools`** (optional): Lists tools Copilot can use without asking each time. Tools not listed prompt for permission. The page's example value is `allowed-tools: shell`.

The Markdown body holds the instructions, examples, and guidelines.

## Supporting files

Supporting files are allowed. When a skill is invoked, Copilot makes every file in the skill's directory available alongside the instructions. The page's examples include scripts, supplementary Markdown files, and other resources, and `SKILL.md` can reference them. The page doesn't mention `scripts/`, `references/`, or `assets/` subfolders.

## Invocation

- **Automatic:** Copilot decides whether to use a skill based on your prompt and the skill's description. When it does, the `SKILL.md` content is added to the agent's context.
- **Manual:** Include the skill name with a leading slash. The page's example is "Use the /frontend-design skill to create a responsive navigation bar in React."

Useful session commands include `/skills list`, `/skills info`, `/skills reload`, `/skills add`, and `/skills remove SKILL-DIRECTORY`. The terminal equivalent is `copilot skill`, with subcommands such as `list`, `add`, `enable`, and `disable`.

## Preview or GA labels

The page doesn't include any preview or GA label.

## Example SKILL.md

The full example is longer than the 125-character limit on quoted source text, so I can't reproduce it verbatim here. Its frontmatter begins with `name: github-actions-failure-debugging`, and its `description` starts with "Guide for debugging failing GitHub Actions workflows."

The body describes a five-step debugging process that uses GitHub MCP Server tools. It lists recent workflow runs, summarizes failed-job logs, fetches full logs if needed, tries to reproduce the failure locally, and then fixes it and verifies the fix before committing. The tools it names are `list_workflow_runs`, `summarize_job_log_failures`, `get_job_logs`, and `get_workflow_run_logs`.

## Adding someone else's skill

1. Download the skill directory and unzip it if needed.
2. Move it to a project or personal skills location.
3. Start a session or run `/skills reload`.
4. Run `/skills info SKILL-NAME` to confirm it loaded.

The page also mentions that `gh skill` in the GitHub CLI can search for, install, update, and publish skills.

## Security note

Pre-approving `shell` or `bash` removes the confirmation step for terminal commands. The page advises doing this only for skills you have reviewed and fully trust.

detail:
**Files loaded automatically**

Per the article, Copilot CLI "discovers repository and agent instruction files in the standard locations," which cover the repository root, the current directory, directories between them, and directories nested along the path of the file being worked on. The table lists these files:

- `$HOME/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md`: "User-level instructions that apply across repositories."
- `$HOME/.copilot/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`: "Modular user-level instructions."
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: "Repository-wide instructions, discovered in the standard locations."
- `.github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md`: "Modular repository instructions, discovered in the standard locations but not intermediate directories."
- `AGENTS.md`: "Agent instructions, discovered in the standard locations."
- `CLAUDE.md`: "Agent instructions, discovered in the standard locations. Copilot CLI also uses `.claude/CLAUDE.md`."
- `GEMINI.md`: "Agent instructions, discovered in the standard locations."

Setting `COPILOT_HOME` changes the home-directory location: "If you set the `COPILOT_HOME` environment variable, Copilot CLI uses that directory instead of `$HOME/.copilot`."

**COPILOT_CUSTOM_INSTRUCTIONS_DIRS**

The table describes the variable's locations as "Directories listed in `COPILOT_CUSTOM_INSTRUCTIONS_DIRS`," which load "Additional `AGENTS.md` and `*.instructions.md` files. Separate multiple directories with commas."

**Precedence and combining**

- The article says "Copilot CLI combines their instructions" when multiple applicable files exist.
- It "removes duplicate copies of identical user-level `copilot-instructions.md`, repository-wide, and agent instructions."
- It states that Copilot CLI "does not define a general precedence order between these files." It advises: "Avoid conflicting instructions."
- Path-specific files are limited by `applyTo`, and "An instruction file that you disable using `/instructions` is not included."

**--no-custom-instructions flag**

The article does not mention this flag, so I can't quote or describe it from this content.

detail:
This page is the GitHub Copilot hooks reference, so it covers your questions. It describes each payload as a JSON object sent to the hook handler but does not say whether command hooks receive it on stdin.

## Configuration file locations (Copilot CLI unless noted)

- **Repository:** `.github/hooks/*.json` in the repo root (also the only location in cloud agent).
- **User:** `*.json` in `~/.copilot/hooks/` (macOS/Linux), `%USERPROFILE%\.copilot\hooks\` (Windows), or `$COPILOT_HOME/hooks/` if `COPILOT_HOME` is set.
- **Inline `hooks` field:** top level of `.github/copilot/settings.json`, `.github/copilot/settings.local.json`, or `~/.copilot/settings.json`. `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json` are also read.
- **Policy:** `/etc/github-copilot/policy.d/*.json` (Linux/macOS) or `C:\ProgramData\GitHub\Copilot\policy.d\*.json` (Windows).
- **Plugins:** `hooks.json` or `hooks/hooks.json` in the plugin's installation directory.

## File schema

"Hook configuration files use JSON format with version `1`."

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "disableAllHooks": false,
  "hooks": {
    "preToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "bash": "YOUR_BASH_COMMAND",
        "powershell": "YOUR_POWERSHELL_COMMAND",
        "cwd": "OPTIONAL/WORKING/DIRECTORY",
        "env": { "VAR": "VALUE" },
        "timeoutSec": 30
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Per-hook command fields:**

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | `"command"`. Defaults to command when omitted. |
| `bash` | Unix shell command. |
| `powershell` | Windows shell command. Ignored in cloud agent. |
| `command` | Cross-platform fallback. |
| `cwd` | "Working directory for the command (relative to repository root or absolute)." |
| `env` | "Environment variables to set (supports variable expansion)." |
| `timeoutSec` | Seconds before the hook is killed. Default `30`. |
| `timeout` | Alias for `timeoutSec`, used only when `timeoutSec` is absent. |
| `exec`, `args` | CLI only. Runs an executable directly without a shell. Cannot be combined with `bash`, `powershell`, or `command`. |

One of `bash`, `powershell`, or `command` is required unless `exec` is set. Other types are `http` (requires `url`) and `prompt` (`sessionStart` only).

## Event names and input payloads

Configure camelCase names to receive camelCase payloads. Configure PascalCase names (for example, `PreToolUse`) to receive snake_case payloads.

| Event (camelCase / PascalCase) | Input fields (camelCase form) |
|---|---|
| `sessionStart` / `SessionStart` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, source (startup/resume/new), initialPrompt? |
| `sessionEnd` / `SessionEnd` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, reason |
| `userPromptSubmitted` / `UserPromptSubmit` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, prompt |
| `userPromptTransformed` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, prompt, transformedPrompt |
| `preToolUse` / `PreToolUse` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, toolName, toolArgs |
| `postToolUse` / `PostToolUse` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, toolName, toolArgs, toolResult |
| `postToolUseFailure` / `PostToolUseFailure` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, toolName, toolArgs, error |
| `agentStop` / `Stop` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, transcriptPath, stopReason, stop_hook_active |
| `subagentStart` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, transcriptPath, agentName, agentDisplayName?, agentDescription? |
| `subagentStop` / `SubagentStop` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, transcriptPath, agentId, agentType, agentName, response, stopReason |
| `errorOccurred` / `ErrorOccurred` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, error, errorContext, recoverable |
| `preCompact` / `PreCompact` | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, transcriptPath, trigger (manual/auto), customInstructions |
| `notification` (CLI only) | sessionId, timestamp, cwd, message, title?, notification_type |

- camelCase `timestamp` is epoch milliseconds. PascalCase `timestamp` is an ISO 8601 string.
- The page lists no input schema for `permissionRequest`.

1	# Project conventions for AI agents
2	
3	Invoice approval demo app: ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with a small static web UI.
4	
5	## Layout
6	
7	- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Domain`: business rules, no web or storage code. `ApprovalService` owns the invoice lifecycle (Draft, PendingApproval, Approved, Rejected).
8	- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api`: controllers, sign-in (`Auth/`), in-memory repository, and the web UI under `wwwroot/`.
9	- `backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests`: xUnit tests, one test class per class under test, named `<ClassUnderTest>Tests`.
10	- `e2e`: Playwright end-to-end tests (`tests/`) and page objects (`pages/`).
11	- `docs/use-cases`: short briefs for features we may build.
12	
13	## Conventions
14	
15	- Controllers live in `Controllers/`, one per resource, route `api/[controller]`. Request bodies are `record` types declared inside the controller.
16	- Controllers inherit `ApiControllerBase` and use `Handle(...)` so service errors map to 404, 409 and 400.
17	- Every endpoint is behind sign-in. Restrict actions with `[RequireRole("...")]`: destructive actions are Admin only, approvals are Approver or Admin.
18	- Business rules go in the Domain project, never in controllers.
19	- Register services in `Program.cs`. Repositories are interfaces in Domain with an in-memory implementation in Api.
20	- Every new rule or endpoint needs tests. Use `FakeInvoiceRepository` in tests.
21	- Use clear names; no one-letter variables or `flag` parameters.
22	- End-to-end tests use page objects and role-based locators (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`), never CSS or XPath selectors.
23	
24	## Commands
25	
26	- Run the app: `dotnet run --project backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api` then open http://localhost:5000
27	- Run the tests: `dotnet test backend/InvoiceApp.sln`
28	- Run end-to-end tests: `cd e2e && npm install && npx playwright install chromium && npm test`
29	
30	## Demo accounts (not real credentials)
31	
32	- `demo.approver` / `ChangeMe123!` (role Approver)
33	- `demo.admin` / `ChangeMe123!` (role Admin)
34	
35	## Never
36	
37	- Commit real credentials, tokens or customer data.
38	- Add business logic to `Program.cs` or controllers.
39

1	# Project conventions for AI agents
2	
3	Invoice approval demo app: ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with a small static web UI and an in-memory store.
4	Read this file before you change anything. Every section is here because an agent arriving cold would otherwise get it wrong.
5	
6	## Approval rules (the contract for approval limits by role)
7	
8	This branch implements approval limits by role. Full spec: `specs/001-role-approval-limits/`. Working notes and test matrix: `.claude/skills/approval-rules/SKILL.md`.
9	
10	| ID | Rule |
11	| --- | --- |
12	| AL-1 | A **Manager** may approve invoices up to **50,000.00** (inclusive). |
13	| AL-2 | A **Director** may approve invoices up to **500,000.00** (inclusive) alone. |
14	| AL-3 | Above **500,000.00** needs **two distinct approvers**, and the **second must be a Director**. The first approval keeps the invoice `PendingApproval` and records who gave it. |
15	| AL-4 | The **same user never counts as both approvers** on one invoice (usernames compared trimmed and case-insensitive). |
16	| AL-5 | A **denied attempt returns a clear reason** (HTTP 403, `{ "error": "<reason>" }`) and **nothing about the invoice changes**. |
17	| AL-6 | A role with no limit (Admin, unknown, empty) **cannot approve**. Fail closed. |
18	
19	AL-4 and AL-5 are where generated code looks right and is not:
20	
21	- The repositories hand out the stored `Invoice` object itself. Setting a field and then throwing **is** a change, even without `Update`. Run every check first; assign fields last.
22	- `firstApprover == approver` lets `Demo.Director` and `demo.director` both approve. Normalise before comparing.
23	
24	## Layering
25	
26	```text
27	wwwroot UI ──HTTP──> Api/Controllers ──> Domain: ApprovalService, ApprovalLimits ──> IInvoiceRepository
28	                     Api/Auth: session -> username + role                         Api: InMemoryInvoiceRepository
29	```
30	
31	- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Domain`: every business rule, the limits table and domain exceptions. No ASP.NET, no storage code.
32	- `backend/src/InvoiceApp.Api`: controllers, sign-in (`Auth/`), the in-memory repository and the web UI (`wwwroot/`). Controllers only translate HTTP to a service call.
33	- The approver's username and role come from the session (`HttpContext.GetSession()`), never from a request body.
34	- `ApiControllerBase.Handle(...)` maps service errors: `KeyNotFoundException` → 404, `InvalidOperationException` → 409, `ArgumentException` → 400. Approval denials get their own exception mapped to 403 with the reason.
35	
36	## Layout
37	
38	- `backend/tests/InvoiceApp.Tests`: xUnit tests, one test class per class under test, named `<ClassUnderTest>Tests`.
39	- `e2e`: Playwright end-to-end tests (`tests/`) and page objects (`pages/`).
40	- `specs/`: Spec Kit specifications, plans and task lists, one folder per feature.
41	- `docs/use-cases`: short briefs for features we may build. `docs/mutation`: recorded Stryker reports.
42	- `.claude/`: agents, skills, hooks and settings for AI agents (see "AI tooling" below). `ai-logs/`: the AI interaction log.
43	
44	## Conventions
45	
46	- Controllers live in `Controllers/`, one per resource, route `api/[controller]`. Request bodies are `record` types declared inside the controller.
47	- Controllers inherit `ApiControllerBase` and use `Handle(...)`.
48	- Every endpoint is behind sign-in. Restrict actions with `[RequireRole("...")]`: destructive actions are Admin only, approvals are Approver or Admin.
49	- Business rules go in the Domain project, never in controllers. Numbers such as 50,000 and 500,000 appear once, in the limits table.
50	- Register services in `Program.cs`. Repositories are interfaces in Domain with an in-memory implementation in Api.
51	- Use clear names; no one-letter variables or `flag` parameters. Money is `decimal`; format it with the invariant culture in messages.
